title: 2D Transport in an in-plane magnetic field
abstract: A parallel in-plane magnetic field could, in principle, distinguish between two competing physical scenarios for the experimentally observed density-tuned 2D metal-insulator transition (where decreasing the carrier density leads to a crossover from an effective metal to an effective insulator): Wigner crystallization or Anderson localization. Since the main scattering mechanism in 2D doped semiconductors arises from screened random charged impurities and screening in turn depends on the electronic density of states, the in-plane magnetic field could distinguish between the two by decreasing screening through spin polarization and this enhances the effective critical density for Anderson localization compared with Wigner crystallization. We give the general theory and provide results for the quantitative magnitudes of the spin polarization effect on the transition density by focusing on two recent experiments [Z. Ge, et al, arXiv:2510.12009, T. Han, et al, arXiv:2604.00113], noting that the critical density may actually decrease if the dominant scattering is by short-ranged defects instead of long-ranged charged impurities. The difference between the two cases arises from whether spin polarization dominates screening (enhanced critical density) or the Fermi surface (suppressed critical density).
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to use an in-plane magnetic field to distinguish between Wigner crystallization and Anderson localization as the cause of a 2D metal-insulator transition. By analyzing how the critical density changes with the applied field, the authors show that the dependence reveals whether disorder or electron correlation dominates the insulating state.
main_problem: The primary goal is to distinguish between two competing mechanisms—Wigner crystallization (WC) or Anderson localization—responsible for the density-tuned Metal-Insulator Transition (MIT) in 2D electron systems.
main_result: Applying a parallel in-plane magnetic field ($B_{||}$) allows differentiation: if the critical density changes with $B$, it suggests disorder-driven localization; if it remains unchanged, it favors WC pinning.
method: The authors develop general theory using Random Phase Approximation (RPA) and Boltzmann transport equations to calculate spin-polarized conductivity ($\sigma$) under an in-plane field.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D doped semiconductor layer with parabolic dispersion, subjected to an in-plane magnetic field that lifts the spin degeneracy via Zeeman coupling. The analysis compares theoretical predictions for WC and Anderson localization criteria.
key_observables: Critical density ($n_{MIT}$), resistivity ($ho$) as a function of $B$ and carrier density ($n$), and the effective degeneracy ($g_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: In-plane magnetic field strength ($B_{||}$), disorder type (short-range vs. long-range Coulomb impurities), and dimensionless Wigner-Seitz radius ($r_S$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the in-plane field only couples via Zeeman coupling, neglecting orbital effects; approximations like strong screening ($\Pi_0$) are used for calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate resistivity vs. $n$ at various fields and disorder strengths, comparing calculated $ho(B)$ curves against the Ioffe-Regel-Mott (IRM) localization criterion boundary.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the theoretical framework for spin polarization effects on screening to deriving transport equations that yield a field dependence of resistivity ($ho(B)$), which is then used diagnostically to distinguish between WC and Anderson MIT mechanisms based on how $n_{MIT}$ responds to $B$.
why_interesting: The work provides a clear diagnostic tool using external fields ($B$) to probe the fundamental nature (disorder vs. correlation) of an electronic phase transition, which is highly relevant for understanding strongly correlated and disordered quantum materials.
